group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 42-year-old man was rushed to the department by co-workers after he collapsed onto a loading dock pallet midway through his afternoon shift at a local electronics warehouse; they report he had spent the previous three days pushing through worsening chills, high-volume sweating, and a hacking cough that produced foul-tasting yellow sputum but refused to seek help because he “couldn’t afford to miss any hours.”  He normally resides in a second-floor walk-up apartment with his partner, climbs two flights of stairs multiple times a day without limitation, and commutes by bicycle when the weather allows; no family members describe baseline confusion or memory lapses.  Past illnesses are few except for chronic transaminitis discovered during a blood donation screening eight years ago and later attributed to untreated hepatitis B acquired perinatally—fibro-scan last year revealed mild portal bridging without evidence of varices, ascites, encephalopathy, or synthetic failure, and he has never required antiviral therapy or hepatology procedural interventions. He denies any prior diagnoses of cancer or congestive heart failure.  He takes no prescription medications, purchases over-the-counter ibuprofen for occasional musculoskeletal aches, drinks two bottles of beer on weekends, and has never smoked or used illicit substances.  Vaccination records in his phone show an inactivated influenza shot from a community drive in November and completion of both pneumococcal series during adolescence because of childhood asthma that resolved by high school.  Paramedics found him seated on the warehouse floor, diaphoretic and panting, alternating between mumbling incoherent phrases and staring blankly; out of concern for preserving pristine vitals they withheld oxygen, intravenous fluids, antipyretics, or nebulizers during the eight-minute transport.  In the resuscitation bay, before any intervention beyond placement of saline locks, he appeared tremulous, skin flushed and hot, pupils equal but slow to track, and answered only to loud voice, misidentifying the month and hospital; Glasgow Coma Scale scored 13 (E3 V4 M6).  Pre-treatment vital signs read: oral temperature 102.0 °F, regular pulse 119 beats per minute, automated right-arm blood pressure 134/81 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute with nasal flaring and visible abdominal displacement, and fingertip pulse oximetry 92 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude.  Neck veins were flat at 30°, the point of maximal impulse was non-displaced, and auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1/S2 without gallop or murmur.  Pulmonary examination demonstrated coarse bronchial breath sounds and inspiratory crackles spanning the entire left upper lobe and lower lobe posteriorly, with resonant percussion tones throughout and no stony dullness or succussion splash to suggest fluid accumulation; the right lung transmitted vesicular sounds with an occasional late crackle at the base.  Abdomen was soft, mildly distended, and revealed a smooth, firm liver edge palpable two centimeters below the costal margin but non-tender; no spider angiomas, caput medusae, or asterixis were elicited.  Extremities were warm without edema, capillary refill under two seconds, and fingernails stained with years of solder flux exposure.  Bedside capillary glucose obtained before phlebotomy measured 158 mg/dL.  Venous blood drawn within five minutes of arrival showed sodium 115 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 88 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 56 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, and serum glucose 154 mg/dL; complete blood count demonstrated leukocytes 18.4 × 10⁹/L with 90 % neutrophils, hematocrit 62 %, hemoglobin 20.0 g/dL, and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L.  An arterial sample from the right radial artery, drawn while he continued to breathe room air, returned pH 7.65, PaCO₂ 24 mm Hg, PaO₂ 94 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 26 mEq/L, and base excess +2, consistent with a primary respiratory alkalosis driven by extreme tachypnea.  Lactate was 1.8 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin fell below the assay detection threshold.  A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes after arrival—prior to fluids, antibiotics, or oxygen—revealed a dense, homogeneous consolidation occupying most of the left upper lobe with prominent air bronchograms; both costophrenic angles remained sharp, cardiac silhouette was normal, mediastinum stable, and no meniscus or layering shadow suggested pleural fluid.  Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 118 bpm with a normal axis and nonspecific anterior T-wave flattening comparable to an occupational health tracing from two years earlier.  Two peripheral blood-culture sets, a coughed sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched before any antimicrobial or supportive therapy was initiated, ensuring that all physiologic measurements and laboratory values above represent the patient’s untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using untreated admission findings.
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age, so 42 years = 42 points. He lives at home, so no nursing-home points (+0).
- Comorbidities: chronic hepatitis B with fibrosis qualifies as liver disease (+20). No malignancy, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, or renal disease is reported (+0 each).
- Examination: new disorientation (+20); respiratory rate 52/min, meeting the ≥30 threshold (+20). Systolic BP 134 mmHg is not <90 (+0); temperature 38.9°C is neither <35 nor ≥40 (+0); pulse 119/min is not ≥125 (+0).
- Laboratory results: BUN 56 mg/dL is ≥30 (+20); sodium 115 mEq/L is <130 (+20). Arterial pH 7.65 is not <7.35 (+0); glucose 154 mg/dL is not ≥250 (+0); hematocrit 62% is not <30% (+0). Room-air PaO₂ 94 mmHg and saturation 92% meet neither hypoxemia threshold (<60 mmHg or <90%, respectively; +0).
- Radiograph: consolidation without pleural effusion (+0).
Total = 42 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 20 = 142.
Final answer: 142
